```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment="#>")
library(coherentSurv)
```

The five revision modules share an interface but retain their own observation
models and numerical diagnostics. This guide uses synthetic data throughout.

## Fit a trajectory law and inspect its assumptions

```{r fit}
d <- cs_simulate(100,horizon=2,seed=72,time_unit="years")
fit <- cs_fit(~x,d,time_unit="years",
                 control=cs_control(history_cap=0,phi_fixed=.4))
fit$convergence$code
summary(fit)$frailty_diagnostics$null_variance_test
```

The gamma law is a working distribution for shared heterogeneity. Other
distributions can be fitted by changing one argument. Lognormal fitting checks
quadrature refinement; discrete fitting estimates normalized support and weights.

```{r alternative}
lnfit <- suppressWarnings(cs_fit(~x,d,time_unit="years",frailty="lognormal",
  control=cs_control(history_cap=0,phi_fixed=.4)))
lnfit$audit$quadrature_refinement
```

A family comparison is available through
`cs_frailty_diagnose(fit, alternatives=TRUE)`. Its AIC values compare fitted
working distributions. They are not a chi-square test of nonnested models.

## Retain uncertainty about an event time

Suppose a recorded recurrence occurred between years 0.2 and 0.4. The person
is known to be alive and followed through year 1. The record below does not
claim that an unmonitored interval contains zero events: its specified count
and mark are complete, while the event time is coarsened.

```{r coarsening}
history <- data.frame(id=901,event_time_lower=.2,event_time_upper=.4,
                      event_type="1",terminal=0,followup=1,x=0)
fibre <- cs_coarsen_fibre(history,event_types=c("1","2"),
                         time_unit="years",nodes=4)
fibre$tie_audit
pred <- predict(fit,newdata=history,landmark=1,horizon=.5,type="all",
                newdata_observation="coarsened")
pred[,c("unit","target","estimate","series_error_bound")]
```

The calculation averages forecasts after posterior updating over each compatible
history. It does not replace the histories by their mean event time.

## Use ordered future covariates

The next example stipulates a covariate update at year 1.25. It is a prediction
scenario, not a causal effect of changing treatment.

```{r schedule}
schedule <- data.frame(id=901,time=1.25,x=1)
predict(fit,history,landmark=1,horizon=.5,type="risk",
        newdata_observation="coarsened",covariate_evolution="locf",
        newdata_future=schedule)
```

For a stochastic longitudinal submodel, fit `cs_covariate_model()` on a training
measurement table. Supply `covariate_history` separately to prediction: interval
boundaries are not repeated biomarker measurements. The model integrates future
Gaussian random-coefficient trajectories and reports Monte Carlo error. It
assumes that future events do not feed back into covariate evolution, conditional
on the supplied past. It is not a joint latent measurement-error survival fit.

## Cross-fit and target continuous-time rewards

The continuous targeting engine uses an explicitly declared sufficient-state,
right-censoring experiment. It does not silently inherit the shared-frailty
likelihood model above. Here the simulator's final event-free interval ending
before the administrative horizon identifies a right-censoring time.

```{r targeting}
d$censored <- as.integer(d$event_type==0 & d$terminal==0 & d$stop<2)
targeted <- suppressWarnings(cs_fit(~x,d,time_unit="years",targeting="continuous",
  control=cs_control(history_cap=1),
  targeting_spec=list(horizon=2,censor="censored",nfolds=3,grid=32)))
summary(targeted)$estimates
predict(targeted,draws=300)
```

Inspect `inference_status` with every interval. A solved EIF equation does not
establish regularity when a mark has no observed events. Boundary outputs use
the stated nonparametric outer-set calculation where available, rather than
presenting a nearly zero standard error as reliable precision. Without a known
upper bound, an uncapped recurrence burden cannot receive a finite upper limit
from a distribution-free bounded-reward argument.

## Use sparse propagation and large-support sensitivity bounds

```{r sparse}
Q <- cs_generator_csr(3,from=c(1,1,2),to=c(2,3,3),rate=c(.3,.1,.2))
cs_propagate_sparse(c(1,0,0),Q,1,reward=c(1,1,0))
p <- rep(1/100,100)
region <- cs_bounds(p,numerator=seq(0,1,length.out=100),
                    kappa=2,recording_fraction=.7)
c(lower=region$lower,upper=region$upper)
region$method
```

The scalable bound solver exploits the specific recording-odds and coarsening
constraints; it is not a general-purpose sparse linear-programming replacement.
Its certificates refer to the numerical finite-support experiment. Observation
assumptions, target definitions and denominator positivity remain part of the
analysis specification.
